SESSION 21 · STUDY NOTES · REV V1

LangGraph human-in-the-loopwith interrupt()

Two new primitives (interrupt, Command), one mandatory plumbing piece (a checkpointer + thread_id), and the gap between “chatbot that needs you present” and “agent that can wait.”

INTERRUPT · COMMAND(RESUME=…) + MEMORYSAVER · THREAD_ID + ONE CRITICAL SECURITY FINDING
interrupt() is not input(). The graph stops, the entire state is checkpointed to a configured store, the Python process can die, restart on another machine, and Command(resume=…) picks up exactly where it left off. That’s the difference between a chatbot and an agentic workflow.

CHECK YOURSELFWhy is “graph pauses and resumes later” a meaningfully different capability from “code blocks on input() until the user types something”?
§ 01 — THE THRESHOLD CONCEPT

What this session exists to flip in your head

THE THRESHOLD CONCEPT

interrupt() is not input(). Python’s input() blocks one thread inside one process until standard input produces a line; nothing about the rest of the program is saved. interrupt() returns control to whoever called graph.invoke(), persists the entire graph state to a checkpointer, and lets the calling program decide whether to resume now, in 5 seconds, in 5 days from a different machine, or never. The interrupt is a yield point in a coroutine, plus a transaction commit, plus a session-id-keyed lookup. It’s a different abstraction layer than input() — and that’s the whole reason LangGraph exists for HITL.

The lecturer says this herself near the end of the session: “Many blogs are also wrong — they will use input. Input and interrupt is very different. Input is a Python function which will allow you to take your input from the keyboard. Interrupt is stopping the workflow. The entire graph is paused there.”

JAVA / SPRING BRIDGE

interrupt() is a coroutine yield + a @Transactional commit. The graph yields back to whoever called invoke(); the state is committed to the checkpointer (the JPA EntityManager analogue); the calling code can resume later — possibly from a different process — via invoke(Command(resume=…)). The combination of “yield” + “persist” + “resume from any process by ID” is what a durable workflow engine (Temporal, AWS Step Functions, Camunda) gives you. LangGraph with interrupt() is in the durable-workflow family, scoped to LLM agentic graphs.

CHECK YOURSELFThree things interrupt() does that input() doesn’t.
§ 02 — THE WORKFLOW

The coding-assistant graph

Goal. Given a coding task (e.g. “write a function to reverse a string”), generate Python code with an LLM, pause and let a human review/edit it, then generate unit tests for the (possibly edited) code.

State schema (a TypedDict carrying three fields):

class CodingAssistantState(TypedDict):
    task: str       # the coding task (mandatory input)
    code: str       # generated/edited Python code
    tests: str      # generated unit tests

The lecturer asks: “which of the three state fields is mandatory when you invoke() the graph?” Only task. The other two start empty and are filled in by the nodes.

CHECK YOURSELFIn this graph, why is the design sequential and not parallel?
§ 03 — NODES, RECAPPED

The shape of a LangGraph node

A node in LangGraph is a Python callable: state → state_update. It receives the current state dict and returns a dict of fields to merge into the state. The lecturer’s generate_code node is the LLM-call shape:

def generate_code(state) -> Command[Literal["human_review"]]:
    """Node 1: Generate Python code using LLM"""
    code = code_chain.invoke({"task": state["task"]})
    return Command(goto="human_review", update={"code": code})

Three pieces:

  1. It reads state. state["task"] pulls the user’s coding question out of the shared state.
  2. It calls a chain. code_chain = code_prompt | model | StrOutputParser() — plain LangChain — produces a string of Python source.
  3. It returns a Command. Bundles “where to go next” (goto="human_review") with “what state field to update” (update={"code": code}). Unpacked in §04.
FAILURE TELLIf a node returns Command(goto="x") and you’ve also declared add_edge(source, "y") for the same source node, both edges fire in parallel — the graph fans out to x and y, which is almost never what you wanted. Pick one routing style per source node — see §08.
CHECK YOURSELFWhy is state["task"] available inside generate_code without ever being passed to it explicitly?
§ 04 — THE COMMAND TYPE

Command(): the new way to bundle “update + goto”

Command is a return-type from LangGraph’s langgraph.types module. It does two jobs at once:

Command(
    goto="next_node_name",     # where to go next
    update={"field": value}    # state fields to merge in
)

The lecturer’s framing: “command is the latest feature of LangGraph … instead of conditional logic, we are kind of giving instruction directly to go to where. If you are using Command, no need to use the add_edge command.”

Two equivalent expressions of the same graph:

# Style A — Command (the lecturer's notebook)
def generate_code(state):
    code = code_chain.invoke({"task": state["task"]})
    return Command(goto="human_review", update={"code": code})

workflow.add_node("generate_code", generate_code)
workflow.set_entry_point("generate_code")
# No add_edge needed — Command does it.

# Style B — add_edge (the classic LangGraph style)
def generate_code(state):
    code = code_chain.invoke({"task": state["task"]})
    return {"code": code}                    # just the update

workflow.add_node("generate_code", generate_code)
workflow.set_entry_point("generate_code")
workflow.add_edge("generate_code", "human_review")   # routing in the builder

Both produce identical runtime behaviour. The lecturer says she prefers Style B but uses Style A in the notebook to introduce the new primitive.

JAVA / SPRING BRIDGE

Think of add_edge as @RequestMapping declared on the controller (routing in the class) versus Command(goto=...) as a method that returns a RedirectView (routing decided inside the method body). Both are valid Spring; they’re stylistically different. Same trade-off here.

Command(goto=END) is how a node says “we’re done.” END is a sentinel imported from langgraph.graph.

Command(resume=...) is not a return value — it’s an input you feed to graph.invoke() to resume after an interrupt. Different use of the same Command class. We’ll see it in §07.

CHECK YOURSELFA node returns Command(goto="x") without an update=… argument. Is that legal? What’s the effect on the graph state?
§ 05 — INTERRUPT

The actual pause

This is the headline new primitive. Inside human_review:

def human_review(state) -> Command[Literal["create_tests"]]:
    # INTERRUPT — this pauses execution and waits for human input
    human_response = interrupt({
        "message": "Please review the generated code below.",
        "code": state["code"],
        "instructions": "Respond with {'action': 'approve'} "
                        "or {'action': 'edit', 'edited_code': '...'}"
    })

    if human_response.get("action") == "edit" and "edited_code" in human_response:
        return Command(goto="create_tests",
                       update={"code": human_response["edited_code"]})
    else:
        return Command(goto="create_tests")

What happens when this runs:

  1. The graph executes generate_code, which fills state["code"] with LLM-generated Python.
  2. The graph transitions to human_review and starts running its body.
  3. interrupt(payload) fires. The payload (a dict) is captured. The graph stops. Execution unwinds back to wherever graph.invoke(...) was called from. The current state is checkpointed.
  4. The invoke() call returns. The return value has an __interrupt__ key containing the payload, so the caller (Jupyter cell, Streamlit app, FastAPI route, whatever) can show the payload to a human and collect a response.
  5. Time passes. The Python process can keep running other invocations; or be killed; or be restarted on another machine; or wait days.
  6. The caller eventually calls graph.invoke(Command(resume=human_response), config={"configurable": {"thread_id": …}}).
  7. The graph wakes up. The line after the interrupt(...) call becomes human_response = <whatever was passed as resume=…>. The body of human_review runs the rest, returns a Command, and execution proceeds to create_tests.

The two things that have to be in place for this to work:

  • The graph must be compiled with a checkpointer: workflow.compile(checkpointer=MemorySaver()). Without one, interrupt() raises an error.
  • The caller must supply a thread_id in config={"configurable": {"thread_id": "..."}}. The thread_id is the key the checkpointer uses to find the right state when you resume.
FAILURE TELLIf you call graph.invoke() on a graph that uses interrupt() but doesn’t have a checkpointer, LangGraph raises a checkpointer-required error. Solution: workflow.compile(checkpointer=MemorySaver()).
FAILURE TELLIf you call graph.invoke(Command(resume=...), config=...) with a thread_id that the checkpointer doesn’t have any state for, the graph starts from scratch — confusingly, because the resume payload is ignored. Solution: use the same thread_id you used on the original invoke().
CHECK YOURSELFWhat’s the payload of interrupt() actually for? Name two things the caller uses it for.
§ 06 — CHECKPOINTERS + THREAD_ID

The persistence layer

The checkpointer is the persistence layer for graph state. Three implementations exist:

CHECKPOINTERWHERE IT LIVESWHEN TO USE
MemorySaver (langgraph.checkpoint.memory)A dict in the running Python processNotebooks, demos, tests. Lost on process exit.
SqliteSaver (langgraph.checkpoint.sqlite)A single SQLite file on diskSingle-process production apps; survives restarts; ~zero ops cost
PostgresSaver (langgraph.checkpoint.postgres)A Postgres tableMulti-process production; horizontally scales; ops cost = your Postgres’

The lecturer uses MemorySaver for the demo and mentions the production options briefly: “you can also use SQLite or any other SQL database where you can save your checkpoints in the backend.”

The thread_id is not a Python threading.Thread and not a Java Thread. It’s a conversation/session identifier — closer to JSESSIONID in a Spring webapp or conversationId in a chat product. The checkpointer keys all state on this id:

thread_config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "coding-session-001"}}

# First invocation — graph runs, hits interrupt, state saved under "coding-session-001"
result = coding_assistant.invoke({"task": task}, config=thread_config)

# Later — same thread_id used to resume from where we left off
final = coding_assistant.invoke(
    Command(resume={"action": "approve"}),
    config=thread_config
)

You can run many independent threads on the same compiled graph. The lecturer demos two different threads (coding-session-001 and coding-session-002) in the same notebook; each holds its own state.

JAVA / SPRING BRIDGE

thread_id is HttpSession#getId(), not Thread#getId(). Multiple users hitting your app simultaneously = multiple LangGraph threads, each with its own state. A JDBC-backed session store ≈ PostgresSaver; a Redis-backed session store ≈ LangGraph’s separate RedisSaver package; in-memory session storage that dies on app restart ≈ MemorySaver.

FAILURE TELLIf you swap MemorySaver for SqliteSaver in production and your application runs on multiple replicas (typical for Kubernetes / Cloud Run), you’ll hit “database is locked” errors. SQLite’s single-writer model breaks under concurrent writers. Move to PostgresSaver (or use session affinity to route by thread_id to the same replica).
CHECK YOURSELFA team uses MemorySaver in production and notices that HITL workflows lose state when their service restarts during a deploy. What’s the fix?
§ 07 — RESUMING

Command(resume=…) — the second half of HITL

After interrupt() has paused the graph and you’ve collected human input, you resume with:

# After collecting human input:
human_response = {"action": "approve"}      # or {"action": "edit", "edited_code": "..."}

final = coding_assistant.invoke(
    Command(resume=human_response),
    config=thread_config                    # SAME thread_id as before
)

Inside the node, the value of human_response inside interrupt(payload) is {"action": "approve"}. Execution picks up at the line after the interrupt(...) call and finishes the node.

Two ways the human responds, in the notebook:

# Path A — approve: no state change, proceed to tests
human_response = {"action": "approve"}

# Path B — edit: replace state["code"] with the human's version
human_response = {
    "action": "edit",
    "edited_code": "def reverse_string(s: str) -> str:\n    return s[::-1]"
}
Correction — the lecturer’s edit-path demo doesn’t do what she expects. The notebook’s Cell 10 sets human_response = {"action": "edit"} without an edited_code field. The human_review function’s condition is action == "edit" AND "edited_code" in human_response — which is False — so it falls through to the else branch (“proceed to tests with no code change”). The lecturer runs this cell and is surprised when the original AI-generated code is used; she blames “Jupyter kernel issues.” The actual bug: {"action": "edit"} without edited_code is structurally indistinguishable from approve, because there’s no edited code to substitute in. The notebook’s separate “ALTERNATIVE: Edit the code before generating tests” cell (Cell 12) is the one that actually exercises the edit path — it includes a real edited_code string. Fix: rename Cell 10 to “APPROVE” so the demo is honest, or change Cell 10 to include a real edited_code payload.
FAILURE TELLIf you send {"action": "edit"} without edited_code, the edit silently doesn’t happen — and the workflow proceeds as if you’d approved. There’s no error. Mitigation in your own code: in human_review, if action == "edit" but edited_code is missing, raise an exception or return back to the interrupt. Don’t fall through silently.
CHECK YOURSELFWhen the user sends Command(resume={"action": "approve"}), what is the value of human_response inside the human_review node?
§ 08 — TWO ROUTING STYLES

When to pick which

STYLEPLAIN ROUTINGCONDITIONAL ROUTING
Inside nodereturn Command(goto="x")return Command(goto="x" if cond else "y")
In builderworkflow.add_edge("a", "b")workflow.add_conditional_edges("a", router_fn)

Style A — Command-driven co-locates routing with state update inside the node. Good for routing that depends on what just happened in this node.

Style B — Edge-driven keeps routing in the graph builder, separate from node bodies. Good when the graph structure is static and worth seeing at a glance.

Pick one style per node (or per graph, if you can). Mixing styles for the same source node makes routing harder to predict.

THE LECTURER’S OWN FRAMING

“Command is a new way in LangGraph. You can also skip command if you’re feeling a little uncomfortable … honestly, I like the kind of node and edge way.” That’s a reasonable take. Style B is more explicit, easier to debug for newcomers, and produces graph visualisations that match the code structure exactly.

CHECK YOURSELFA graph has 7 nodes. Five have a single static next node; one branches on the LLM’s classification; one returns to itself in a retry loop. Which routing style would you reach for first?
§ 09 — THE TIMELINE

Interrupt + resume in one picture

Things worth noticing:

  • “Process can die” is the load-bearing claim of HITL. Swap MemorySaver for SqliteSaver/PostgresSaver and that line goes from aspirational to operational.
  • State strictly accumulates in the example — task added at t=0, code added in generate_code, code possibly overwritten in human_review, tests added in create_tests.
  • Two invoke() calls happen, with different arguments — the first carries the initial input, the second carries Command(resume=…). Same compiled graph object.
JAVA / SPRING BRIDGE

Same shape as a durable workflow — Temporal, Cadence, AWS Step Functions, Camunda. The “state survives process death and resumes from a stable id” pattern is the same; LangGraph’s surface area is just a lot smaller and LLM-aware.

CHECK YOURSELFWhy is it safe for the Python process to die between t=0 and t=N when using SqliteSaver, but not safe when using MemorySaver?
§ 10 — THE NOTEBOOK + SECURITY

The runnable notebook, and a CRITICAL security finding

The lecturer’s runnable notebook lives at:

/Users/manjunathans/projects/SasmitaCourse/Langgraph/
  coding_assistant_HumanIntheLoop_PersistentMemorypnotebook.py

Security finding — a live OpenAI API key is committed to the source

CRITICAL — the notebook contains a real OpenAI API key in plaintext as its first cell. The line is OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-proj-WJ9z3xq3I7PQ51RaPOt…" (truncated here — the key is not reproduced in these notes). This is the canonical OWASP LLM06: Sensitive Information Disclosure finding from the Session 2 Responsible AI catalogue. Anyone with read access to the Langgraph/ folder can use this key to spend the lecturer’s OpenAI credit.

Action:

  1. Revoke the key immediately at platform.openai.com/api-keys. OpenAI’s “Revoke” button invalidates the key instantly.
  2. Issue a new key and store it only in a .env file (or a secrets manager — AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, HashiCorp Vault). Add .env to .gitignore.
  3. Delete the hardcoded line from Cell 1 of the notebook. The notebook already includes the right pattern just below that line — load_dotenv(override=True) reads OPENAI_API_KEY from a .env file — but the hardcoded literal above it overrides everything. Removing the hardcoded line is sufficient.
  4. Audit any other notebooks in this folder and any other shared drives for the same pattern. Once an engineer establishes a habit, the same mistake usually appears in multiple files.

This is exactly the kind of finding the OWASP LLM Top 10 v1 LLM06 / v2 LLM02 (Sensitive Information Disclosure) category was designed for — and it’s a real-world incident-in-the-making whose blast radius is the lecturer’s API spend until the key is rotated.

The “edit” demo cell doesn’t actually edit the code

The notebook’s Cell 10 is labelled “STEP 2 — Provide Human Response (APPROVE)” in its markdown comment, but the actual code is human_response = {"action": "edit"}. With action == "edit" but no edited_code field, the condition falls through. Lecturer runs this cell, expects to see edited code, and is surprised that the original AI code is used. She blames Jupyter; the actual issue is in the cell itself. See §07’s correction. The notebook’s Cell 12 (the “ALTERNATIVE: Edit the code before generating tests”) does include a real edited_code payload and works as expected.

How to run the notebook safely (after the key is rotated)

  1. Create a .env file in Langgraph/: OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-proj-<your-new-key>
  2. Add .env to .gitignore.
  3. Delete Cell 1’s hardcoded literal. Keep the load_dotenv() lines.
  4. Activate the right Python environment (conda activate genai — see ANN-Session 4 §11).
  5. Open the notebook in Jupyter. Run cells in order. At Cell 8 the graph will pause; at Cell 9 you’ll see the interrupt payload; at Cell 10 you respond.
CHECK YOURSELFWhy does the .env pattern work even though the notebook is still in a public folder?
§ 11 — DIAGNOSTIC TABLE

Symptom → cause → first move

SYMPTOMLIKELY CAUSEFIRST MOVE
ValueError: Cannot use interrupt() without a checkpointerGraph compiled without checkpointer=…workflow.compile(checkpointer=MemorySaver())
invoke(Command(resume=...)) starts from scratchDifferent thread_id than the original invoke()Reuse the same thread_id
{"action": "edit"} without edited_code — workflow proceeds as if approvedMissing field; condition falls throughAlways include edited_code when action == "edit"; raise if missing
HITL workflow loses state after restartMemorySaver is in-process onlySwap for SqliteSaver (single replica) or PostgresSaver (multi-replica)
“database is locked” with SqliteSaver in K8sSQLite single-writer breaks under concurrent replicasPostgresSaver, or route by thread_id with session affinity
Two users sharing a thread_id see each other’s statethread_id is keyed by conversation, not userGenerate thread_id per user-conversation
Resume payload right but node doesn’t see itUsed Command(goto=...) in resume call instead of Command(resume=...)Use resume=, not goto=
Graph routes to two destinations from one source unexpectedlyMixed routing styles: Command(goto="x") in the node AND add_edge(source, "y") in the builder, both firePick one style per source node; remove the redundant edge
Notebook commits a real API keyHardcoded literal alongside load_dotenv() — the literal winsDelete the literal; rotate the key; commit .env.example not .env
§ 12 — QUIZ YOURSELF

Ten questions

Recall

  1. State the difference between Python’s input() and LangGraph’s interrupt() in two sentences each.
  2. Name the three checkpointer implementations and when to use each.
  3. What does thread_id identify? What does it not identify?

Application

  1. You’re building a multi-step legal-document drafter where a human must approve each section before the LLM moves to the next. Sketch the LangGraph state schema (what fields) and node structure (what nodes).
  2. You’re running a HITL workflow on Kubernetes with three replicas. Your team uses MemorySaver and reports occasional state-loss bugs. Diagnose and propose two fixes (in order of preference).
  3. A node returns Command(goto="end", update={"answer": x}). The graph builder also has add_edge("this_node", "next_node") declared for the same source node. What happens at runtime?
  4. The notebook leaks an API key on its first cell. The team revokes the key. A junior engineer asks: “why can’t we just keep the key out of git but leave it in the file?” What’s the right answer?

Debugging

  1. A user reports: “I clicked approve on the code review form 3 hours ago, came back from lunch, and the workflow says it never received my response.” You check the logs and see the resume invoke() did fire. What’s the most likely bug?
  2. A human_review node’s body looks correct, but after interrupt() is called the graph errors with “no checkpointer configured.” Where is the fix, and why does it have to be there and not in the node?
  3. Plain-English chain. You’re building a customer-support agent. It takes a ticket; runs an LLM to draft a response; pauses for a human agent to approve or edit; then sends the response and closes the ticket. (i) Which LangGraph primitive pauses the workflow? (ii) Which primitive resumes it? (iii) What’s stored under the thread_id while the workflow is paused? (iv) What happens if the customer-support web server restarts during the pause and you’re using MemorySaver?
ANSWERS
  1. input() blocks one Python thread on stdin; nothing about the program state is saved; if the process dies, the prompt is lost. interrupt() returns control to the caller of graph.invoke() and persists the entire graph state via the checkpointer; the calling process can die and a different process can resume with the same thread_id.
  2. MemorySaver (in-process dict; lost on exit; for demos and tests). SqliteSaver (single SQLite file; survives restarts; single-process production). PostgresSaver (Postgres table; multi-process production; horizontal scale).
  3. Identifies a conversation/session (like JSESSIONID). Does not identify a Python or OS thread.
  4. State: task, sections_completed (list), current_section (int), drafted_text (str), approved_text (str). Nodes: draft_section (LLM call), human_review (interrupt), advance_to_next_section or finalise.
  5. MemorySaver is in-process — replica restart loses state. Fixes: (1) PostgresSaver (works under concurrent replicas, durable). (2) SqliteSaver + session affinity (route same thread_id to same replica).
  6. Both edges fire in parallel — the graph fans out to both "end" and "next_node". That’s almost never the intended behaviour and is a real source of confusing bugs. Fix: pick one style per source node — either return Command(goto=...) from the node or declare add_edge(...) in the builder, never both for the same source.
  7. Three reasons: (1) git-ignore is process discipline, not security — the file still exists on disk wherever the codebase is checked out, each a copy of the key. (2) The notebook is shared via Google Drive; it’s already disclosed. (3) load_dotenv() from a separate .env file lets each developer / environment have its own key without ever putting the value in committed code.
  8. Most likely: the resume invoke() was called with a different thread_id than the original. The graph started fresh under the new id instead of resuming. Fix: ensure the resume call uses the exact same thread_id.
  9. The fix is in the graph compilation step (workflow.compile(checkpointer=MemorySaver())), not in the node. The node only uses the checkpointer; the checkpointer is configured at graph-construction time. Putting it elsewhere would be like trying to enable JPA inside a single @Transactional method.
  10. (i) interrupt(). (ii) Command(resume=...) passed as the first argument to invoke(). (iii) The entire graph state — task, drafted text, customer context, anything in the TypedDict — keyed by thread_id. (iv) State is lost; the human agent’s approval will arrive at a fresh graph that has no memory of the original ticket. Need SqliteSaver or PostgresSaver.

§ 13 — GLOSSARY

The vocabulary of this session

Checkpoint
A snapshot of the graph’s state at a particular node boundary. Created automatically by LangGraph when a checkpointer is configured.
Checkpointer
The object that stores checkpoints. MemorySaver (in-process), SqliteSaver (file), PostgresSaver (database). Required for interrupt().
Command()
A return type from langgraph.types. Bundles routing (goto=...) and state update (update={...}) into one return value from a node.
Command(resume=...)
A different use of the same Command class. Passed as the first argument to invoke() to resume after an interrupt(). The ... becomes the return value of interrupt() inside the node.
configurable config block
The dict you pass to invoke(config=...) to set runtime values like thread_id. Schema: {"configurable": {"thread_id": "...", "checkpoint_id": "..."}}.
HITL — human-in-the-loop
A workflow that pauses for human input and resumes once the input arrives. In LangGraph, implemented with interrupt() + a checkpointer + a thread_id.
interrupt()
A function from langgraph.types. Called from inside a node body; pauses the graph; returns control to the caller of invoke(); the payload (a dict) is delivered to the caller via the __interrupt__ key on invoke()’s return value.
LangGraph
Graph-based orchestration library for agentic LLM workflows. Built on LangChain.
MemorySaver
In-process checkpointer. Fast, zero ops cost, lost on process exit. Demo/notebook use only. (Newer LangGraph versions also export this as InMemorySaver — same class, friendlier name.)
PostgresSaver
Postgres-backed checkpointer (langgraph.checkpoint.postgres). Multi-process production. Survives restarts; scales horizontally.
SqliteSaver
SQLite-backed checkpointer (langgraph.checkpoint.sqlite). Single-process production. File on disk; survives restarts; doesn’t work across replicas due to SQLite’s single-writer limitation.
StateGraph
The LangGraph graph builder. Construct with a state schema (a TypedDict); call add_node, add_edge, set_entry_point, then compile(checkpointer=...).
thread_id
A conversation/session identifier. Passed in the configurable config block on invoke(). The checkpointer keys state by this id. Not a Python or OS thread.
